# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
# Review: "Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations"

This report does what the field needed. It responds to earlier objections, including several raised in this thread:

- **Hours measurement.** It adds a second, system-log measure of hours.
- **Meetings.** It registers the meetings mediation test before the 24-month data existed.
- **Decay.** It reports the decline in the per-hour gain rather than burying it.
- **Meta-analysis.** It checks the meta-analysis's long-follow-up studies against their actual designs. Confirming that all four were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours settles that dispute.

The arithmetic checks out. 0.966/0.88 gives +9.8% and 0.966/0.89 gives +8.5%. For the Halden subset, 34.9/40.3 is −13.4%, and 0.968/0.866 is +11.8%.

The main problems are a confound in the decay comparison that the report itself documents, some overstatement in the Summary, and a definitional question about log hours that affects the mediation result.

## 1. The control offices' meeting audit confounds the decay estimate

In month 15, two of the seven control offices cut their meetings and saw output per hour rise 4.1%. That is contamination of the control arm. It plausibly results from the trial itself, since the nine-month report publicised the meetings finding.

This matters because the 24-month estimate is a difference-in-differences. If control offices improved, the gap narrows even if treated offices held steady. Part of the decline from 12.5% to 9.8% may therefore be control-arm catch-up rather than fading in the treated offices. The report presents the observation as evidence about reorganisation but never connects it to the decay finding.

Needed:
- treated and control trajectories reported separately;
- a sensitivity analysis excluding the two audited offices, or the post-audit months.

The observation also cuts both ways for the meetings story. It suggests some of the gain is available without cutting hours, which the authors say carefully. It also means the 24-month treatment effect understates the full gain of the hours cut plus reorganisation, relative to an untouched control.

## 2. The Summary overstates the decline by mixing measures

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data." The 12.5% is a timesheet figure, and log data didn't exist at nine months. The like-for-like comparison is **12.5% → 9.8%**, as the body correctly says.

Section 5's "declined by about a quarter" is also inexact:

| Comparison | Relative decline |
|---|---|
| Timesheet to timesheet (12.5% → 9.8%) | About a fifth (22%) |
| Timesheet to log (12.5% → 8.5%) | About a third (32%) |

Neither is a quarter.

The two intervals also overlap heavily: +6.9 to +18.4 versus +4.6 to +15.2. The decline itself isn't statistically established. Report a CI for the change, and describe the decline as "consistent with some fading," as Section 3 already does.

## 3. What do log hours measure? This matters for the mediation result

"Active log-in time on the case-management system" sounds like time spent working on cases, not total working time. That raises two questions:

- **Is it the same construct as timesheet hours?** If log time excludes meetings, phone calls and other off-system work, it measures something different. A smaller fall in log hours (−11%) than in timesheet hours (−12%) is then not evidence of unrecorded work. Treated offices cut about 3.5 hours of meetings a week, so their case-work time *should* fall less than their total time.
- **Can meetings mediate output per log hour?** If meeting time sits outside log hours, cutting meetings can't directly raise output per log hour. It can only free time, which shows up as more log hours. A 47% mediated share would then need a different mechanism, such as fewer interruptions or less task-switching, and the paper should say so.

If staff stay logged in during meetings, the issue largely disappears. Either way, define the measure precisely.

A rough cross-check: on timesheet hours, non-meeting time is about 29.5 hours in treated offices and 30.9 in control. Output per non-meeting hour then differs by only about +1%. A simple time-accounting would credit meetings with most of the gain, more than the 47% the model finds. Reconciling these figures would strengthen the mediation section.

## 4. "Confirms" is too strong for the mediation test

The registration is a real improvement, but several limits remain:

- **Same offices, new months.** The hypothesis came from these seven treated offices, and the test uses the same offices with later data. That is a pre-specified test, not an independent replication. Varga–Holm's objection was specifically about replication, so answer it on those terms.
- **Effective sample size.** "A larger sample of office-months" doesn't increase the number of independent units, which remains 7 versus 7. Mediated-share CIs of ±19 points look narrow for 14 clusters. State how clustering was handled and whether small-cluster corrections were applied.
- **Assumptions.** Mediators aren't randomised, so causal mediation requires no unmeasured confounding of mediator and outcome, as the Limitations note. "Supports" is the defensible verb; "confirms" is not.
- **Baseline meeting data.** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six. Where do the baseline figures (7.4 and 7.2 hours) come from? If they were reconstructed retrospectively from calendar history, say so.

## 5. Two outcomes from the nine-month report are still missing

- **Backlogs and deadlines.** The nine-month Limitations flagged the risk that backlogs would build beyond statutory deadlines. Output per FTE has now been 2–3% below control for two years, which implies a growing backlog unless inflow fell. Report backlog size, case age and deadline compliance.
- **Case-processing costs.** The report costs the counter arm (+9% per contact) but not case processing. Hourly pay is up 25% and about 3 hours of weekly overtime continued. Cost per case is the county's actual decision variable.

The appeal-overturn rates are also still month-24 levels with no difference-in-differences estimate or CI.

## 6. The Halden subset

- **Response bias.** 14 of 23 organisations responded. Non-responders may include other reverters or poor performers. Say what is known about the nine who didn't respond.
- **Baseline hours.** 40.3 is the 27-organisation time-tracking average from Varga–Holm. Is it also the baseline for these 11? Do all 11 have time tracking? Only 17 of the 23 had both records and tracking.
- **The marketing agency.** A marketing agency citing client deadlines doesn't fit the review's coverage-bound category. It is closer to discretionary work under external deadlines. The Summary's "all with client-facing or coverage obligations" absorbs it into a broader category. It is better reported as a discretionary-sector reversion, which is informative in its own right.
- **Intention to treat.** Including the three reverters, with output indices of 88–91, alongside the survivors would give a figure for everyone followed up, not just those who continued. The "upper bound" framing is good, and an all-respondents figure would make it concrete.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Counter arm.** The months 10–12 comparison (7.3 vs 4.0 minutes, treated vs control) is a welcome improvement over the earlier before/after figures. Contact volumes by arm are still not reported, so the spillover question from the nine-month report remains open.
- **Sick days.** The −27% still needs the days-versus-hours clarification.
- **The Halden co-author.** With R. Okafor as a co-author, it would be appropriate to acknowledge that the original Halden working paper's "sector-general" conclusion and its description of withdrawals have not held up. The report currently addresses only the re-analysis and the meta-analysis.

## Where the evidence now stands

Across the five documents, the best-supported picture is now fairly clear:

- **Discretionary work.** A per-hour gain of roughly 8–10% persists to two years in the one randomised long-term study. Output per employee falls slightly, and some of the gain may come from reorganisation rather than rest.
- **Coverage-bound work.** Output falls and service worsens enough that the county abandoned the scheme.

Each of the original claims needs qualifying:

- **"Sector-general" (Halden).** Wrong.
- **"Entirely an artifact" (Varga–Holm).** Wrong.
- **"No sign of decay" (the meta-analysis).** Unsupported.

The open question this report correctly identifies is whether reorganisation without an hours cut would capture most of the gain. Answering it needs a three-arm trial: hours cut, reorganisation only, and control.
